sentences.text: This ramp reads a1, a2, a3, a4 and a6. It acts on 206 of 345 training cases, 78 of which are actually 'yes'; for the typical case it acts on (no attribute at its first value: a1 = 2, a2 = 3, a3 = 2, a4 = 2, a5 = 4, a6 = 2), it takes the predicted probability of 'yes' from about 72% without it to above 99% with it.
Through it, a1 = 2, a3 = 2 or a6 = 2 instead of the first value takes the typical case's predicted probability of 'yes' from below 1% to above 99%.
With this part in place, a1 = 3 instead of 1 takes the typical case from below 1% to above 99% when a3 = 1 or a6 = 1; when a3 = 2 or a6 = 2 the prediction is above 99% either way.
Through it, a1 = 3 instead of 1 and giving a2 or a4 its first value lower the probability, though for the typical case it stays below 1%.

This part adds up all six attributes with fixed weights. Through it, a1 = 3 instead of 1 raises the typical case's predicted probability of 'yes' from below 1% to above 99% and a1 = 2 to about 75%, and a5 = 2 instead of 1 raises it to about 93%, a5 = 3 to about 55% and a5 = 4 to about 3%.
Through it, a4 = 1, a3 = 2 and a6 = 2 lower the probability and a2 = 1 or 2 instead of 3 raises it, though for the typical case it stays below 1%.
Across the whole model, a5 = 2 instead of 1 takes the typical case to about 93%, a5 = 3 to about 55% and a5 = 4 to about 1%; a4 = 1 lowers it and a2 = 2 instead of 3 raises it, below 1%.

This small unit reads a5 and a3. It acts on 259 of 345 training cases, 82 of which are actually 'yes'; for the typical case it acts on, the predicted probability of 'yes' stays below 1% with or without it.
Through it, a5 = 4 and a3 = 2 lower the probability, though for the typical case it stays below 1%.
A tiny unit on a6 barely changes the predictions.

lead.text: For the typical case (the most common value of each attribute: a1 = 1, a2 = 3, a3 = 1, a4 = 2, a5 = 1, a6 = 1) the model gives a predicted probability of 'yes' below 1%, and a1 = 2 instead of 1 raises it to above 99%; it adds up four parts: a ramp that falls as more attributes take their first value, a direct sum over all six attributes, a small unit on a5 and a3, and a tiny unit on a6.

evidence.text: It acts on 206 of 345 training cases, 78 of which are actually 'yes'; for the typical case it acts on (no attribute at its first value: a1 = 2, a2 = 3, a3 = 2, a4 = 2, a5 = 4, a6 = 2), it takes the predicted probability of 'yes' from about 72% without it to above 99% with it.
Through it, a1 = 2, a3 = 2 or a6 = 2 instead of the first value takes the typical case's predicted probability of 'yes' from below 1% to above 99%.
With this part in place, a1 = 3 instead of 1 takes the typical case from below 1% to above 99% when a3 = 1 or a6 = 1; when a3 = 2 or a6 = 2 the prediction is above 99% either way.
Through it, a1 = 3 instead of 1 and giving a2 or a4 its first value lower the probability, though for the typical case it stays below 1%; a1 = 3 also counts more when a4 = 1 or a2 = 1.
Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 345 training cases.

hypothesis.text: This ramp gives 'yes' while few of a1, a2, a3, a4 and a6 take their first value: for the typical case, moving a1, a3 or a6 away from its first value takes the predicted probability of 'yes' from below 1% to above 99% through it.

evidence.text: It acts on 259 of 345 training cases, 82 of which are actually 'yes'; for the typical case it acts on, the predicted probability of 'yes' stays below 1% with or without it.
Through it, a5 = 4 and a3 = 2 lower the probability, though for the typical case it stays below 1%.
With this part in place, a3 = 2 instead of 1 takes the typical case from about 1% to above 99% when a5 = 4, and from below 1% to above 99% otherwise.
Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 345 training cases.

hypothesis.text: This small unit reads a5 and a3: through it, a5 = 4 and a3 = 2 lower the probability of 'yes', though for the typical case it stays below 1%.

evidence.text: It acts on the 168 of 345 training cases with a6 = 2, 58 of which are actually 'yes'; for the typical case it acts on, the predicted probability of 'yes' is above 99% with or without it.
Through it, a6 = 2 instead of 1 raises the probability, though for the typical case it stays below 1%.
Switching it off barely changes the predictions.
Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 345 training cases.

hypothesis.text: This tiny unit on a6 barely changes the predictions.

evidence.text: Through it, a1 = 3 instead of 1 raises the typical case's predicted probability of 'yes' from below 1% to above 99% and a1 = 2 to about 75%, and a5 = 2 instead of 1 raises it to about 93%, a5 = 3 to about 55% and a5 = 4 to about 3%.
Through it, a4 = 1, a3 = 2 and a6 = 2 lower the probability and a2 = 1 or 2 instead of 3 raises it, though for the typical case it stays below 1%.

parts.name: upper_edge_count_classifier
parts.original_hypothesis: Hypothesis: additive composition under the output sigmoid, logit = 2.58 + Linear + 5.14*Ramp + 1.53*A5not4 + 0.105*A6. a4:2, a4:3, a5:3 have no enabled connections (zero-effect entries). The model is an upper-edge-only count detector: for a1 in {1,2} it is positive while few attributes take their first value and negative once about three of {a2,a3,a4,a6} (a1=1) or four (a1=2) do; a5=1 counts only through Linear's -14.8, which is not enough to flip a1=1 inputs with one other first value. There is no lower edge: inputs with zero or one first value get the largest logits. a1=3 inputs are all positive (107/107 on train) via Linear's +24.9. Evidence (train, n=345): positive rate by (a1, count) - a1=1: count<=2 100%, 3 74%, >=4 0%; a1=2: count<=3 100%, 4 29%, 5 0%; a1=3: 100% at every count. Predicts positive on 85.5% of train rows (accuracy 0.472 at 0.5). Logits reach |~130| so the sigmoid saturates; the sigmoid-output AUC 0.807 is inflated by ties at 1.0, the logit ranking AUC is 0.734. Compared with the MONK-2 target (exactly two first values): the network captures only the upper edge (>=3-4 first values -> negative) and none of the lower edge (0-1 -> negative), and ignores the count entirely when a1=3.

reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient)

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients
